kurz: Why a comparison of buying and renting is about occupancy costs and not the loan instalment, and why it has to include the return that the equity would have earned elsewhere.

bloecke.md:
The saying “rent is money thrown away” is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Buying also involves money flowing out that does not build wealth: interest to the bank, maintenance to tradespeople, incidental purchase costs to the federal state, the notary and the estate agent. Only one part of the monthly instalment, the repayment, turns into wealth, and this part does not belong in a cost calculation.

A clean comparison therefore sets occupancy costs against occupancy costs, not the instalment against the rent. On one side is everything that is used up when living in your own property, on the other the net basic rent of a comparable flat. Costs that arise in the same amount on both sides are left out. These include heating, water and refuse collection, and also property tax (Grundsteuer), which under the Operating Costs Ordinance (Betriebskostenverordnung) is recoverable from tenants. If property tax is attributed to the buyer alone, the comparison is skewed against buying.

With repayment, money flows from the account into reducing the debt without being used up. It therefore belongs in the balance sheet of your wealth, not in the cost calculation. The cost comparison includes loan interest, maintenance, non-recoverable management costs, the incidental purchase costs spread over the holding period and the return that the equity invested would have earned elsewhere.

## Price-to-rent ratio and gross rental yield

The [[Price-to-rent ratio|price-to-rent ratio]], also called the multiplier (Vervielfältiger), is the purchase price divided by the annual net basic rent. It can be determined as a first indicator even before a viewing and is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A factor of 25 corresponds to 4%, a factor of 40 to only 2.5%.

The calculation uses the net basic rent. A calculation with the rent including heating makes the property look cheaper than it is, because operating costs bring the owner no income. The owner pays them as well, just directly. The factor is not yet a valuation of the property, but it does set a limit. It shows the highest ongoing return the property can deliver before maintenance, management and vacancy are deducted.

bloecke.formel:
Price-to-rent ratio = Purchase price / Annual net basic rent
Gross rental yield = 100 / Price-to-rent ratio
bloecke.erklaerung: Both indicators contain the same information. The factor is common in conversation; the yield allows a comparison with other investments.
variablen: purchase price alone, excluding incidental purchase costs
12 monthly rents excluding operating and heating costs

bloecke.md:
## Model case: an owner-occupied flat

The model case is an owner-occupied flat of 100 square metres, built around the year 2000, with a purchase price of €400,000. The incidental purchase costs consist of 6.5% real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer), around 1.5% for the notary and land register and 3.5% as a half share of the estate agent's commission under Sections 656c and 656d BGB (Civil Code), a total of €46,000 or 11.5%. The €46,000 in incidental costs is deducted from the equity of €126,000, and €80,000 goes into the purchase price. The loan amounts to €320,000, which is 80% of the purchase price. The [[Loan-to-value ratio (Beleihungsauslauf)|loan-to-value ratio (Beleihungsauslauf)]] is higher, because the bank relates the loan to the mortgage lending value, which it sets cautiously and usually below the purchase price.

The calculation assumes 4.0% interest and a 2% initial repayment rate. This interest rate is close to the offer rate of 3.97% effective for a ten-year fixed-rate period that Dr. Klein published at the beginning of September 2026. The [[Annuity|annuity]] is therefore 6% of €320,000, that is, €19,200 a year or €1,600 a month. Of this, €12,800 goes on interest and €6,400 on repayment in the first year.

The forgone return on the €126,000 in equity is set at 4.0% before tax. After the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] for equity funds (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act) and [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] of 26.375% including solidarity surcharge (Section 32d EStG, Income Tax Act; Section 4 SolzG 1995, Solidarity Surcharge Act), around 3.3% of this remains, that is, about €4,100 a year. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG) is not taken into account here. It would increase the amount slightly in the first years. For maintenance, Section 28 of the Second Computation Ordinance (II. BV) applies; its rates have been adjusted to the consumer price index every three years since 2005. Since 1 January 2026, the rate has been €14.58 per square metre per year for buildings between 22 and 31 years old, so €1,458 here.

bloecke.md:
In the first year, occupancy costs of €23,258 for ownership compare with €16,000 in rent. Ownership therefore costs €7,258 more than renting. That alone is not yet an argument against buying, because the figure only describes the starting point. Two developments in the following years are not yet included in it.

First, the interest portion falls because the outstanding balance falls. Averaged over ten years, interest comes to around €11,500 instead of €12,800. However, this saving is almost entirely offset, because the equity tied up in the property grows with every repayment instalment, and with it the forgone return, which reaches around €6,600 in the tenth year. Over the ten years, occupancy costs therefore remain close to €23,300. Second, rents rise while the interest burden does not. The advantage of buying arises from this difference, not from the first year.

If the rent rises by 2% a year, the net basic rent averages around €17,500 over the ten years instead of €16,000. The gap to the housing costs of around €23,300 thus narrows to about €5,800 a year. Over ten years, this adds up to around €58,000.

For buying to draw level, the flat must gain these €58,000 in value within ten years. That is around 14.5%, or just under 1.4% a year, not yet including selling costs. For comparison, prices for residential property in Germany rose by around 82% from 2010 to 2025. In the second quarter of 2026, however, the house price index was only 0.6% above the previous year, after 1.2% in the quarter before. An increase in value of this order of magnitude is therefore achievable, but not certain.

Real estate transfer tax, notary, land register and estate agent's commission do not increase the mortgage lending value of the property. As soon as the notary has notarised the contract, they are sunk costs. A buyer who resells the flat the next day at the same price has lost €46,000.

Two conclusions follow from this. First, this amount has to be earned back over the holding period, and the shorter the holding period, the more heavily it weighs on each individual year. Second, the incidental costs should be paid from equity. Buyers who finance them as well start with a loan-to-value ratio above 100% and pay a noticeable interest rate premium for it. How high the incidental costs turn out also depends on the federal state. Real estate transfer tax ranges from 3.5% in Bavaria to 6.5% in North Rhine-Westphalia, Brandenburg, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein. On €400,000, that is €14,000 compared with €26,000.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the same flat with holding periods of different lengths. If the flat is sold after three years, the incidental purchase costs alone account for €1,278 a month.

bloecke.md:
## Mobility of tenants and owners

A tenant can give notice with a notice period of three months (Section 573c BGB). A buyer can only get out of the loan before the end of the fixed-rate period by paying an early repayment charge. The special right of termination under Section 489(1) no. 2 BGB, which cannot be excluded by contract, only applies ten years after the loan has been paid out in full, with six months' notice and without compensation. On top of this comes the sale itself, with marketing time, possibly an estate agent's commission and a market situation that does not follow your own timetable.

No general rule follows from this, but a condition for buying does. For buyers who expect to change job or city within five years, their own expectation argues against buying. The holding period affects the result of this calculation more than any other variable, more even than half a percentage point on the interest rate.

## Fivefold leverage and cluster risk

After the purchase, €80,000 of the buyer's own money is in the property, because the €46,000 in incidental costs has been used up. The property is worth €400,000, which corresponds to leverage of five to one. If the price falls by 10%, €40,000 is lost, that is, half of the equity invested in the property. In a portfolio, such a position would be a gross violation of every diversification rule. It would be a single, illiquid and debt-financed investment in a single location, often amounting to a multiple of the remaining wealth. With an owner-occupied home, this concentration is considered normal because it comes with living there. That explains it, but it does not reduce the risk.

The increase in value of an owner-occupied flat is tax-free on sale. Under Section 23(1) no. 1 sentence 3 EStG, properties that were occupied by the owner in the year of sale and the two preceding years are exempt; otherwise the ten-year period applies. The return that a tenant earns in a portfolio, by contrast, is taxed on an ongoing basis and not only on sale. For accumulating funds, the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) is due every year (Section 18 InvStG). It is calculated from the base interest rate (Basiszins) of 3.20% as of 2 January 2026, multiplied by 0.7, and is capped at the increase in value achieved during the year.

The illustrative calculation already contains this difference, which is why the forgone return is set at 3.3% instead of 4.0%. The tax advantage also explains part of what owners describe in hindsight as “the house paid off”.

bloecke.titel: Limits of common rules of thumb
bloecke.md:
The rule “pay no more than 20 times the annual rent” dates from a time when mortgage loans carried different interest rates. At a mortgage rate of 2%, even a factor of 35 was sustainable; at 4%, a factor of 30 is already tight. An upper limit for the factor is therefore only meaningful together with the interest rate.

Conversely, the rule “the instalment is just like rent” does not work either. It leaves out maintenance, forgone return and incidental costs, and instead counts repayment as a cost. By coincidence, these two errors partly cancel each other out and therefore go unnoticed for a long time.

One argument cannot be captured in any calculation. The annuity loan enforces saving. Households that, without this compulsion, would spend the difference instead of investing it are better off with ownership after twenty years, even if the calculation shows the opposite. This argument concerns behaviour, not return. It is nevertheless valid, but must not be mistaken for a return.

mitnehmen: The comparison sets the occupancy costs of ownership (interest, maintenance, management, spread incidental purchase costs and forgone return on equity) against the net basic rent, not the instalment against the rent.
Repayment is a reallocation of wealth and does not belong in the cost calculation; recoverable operating costs and property tax arise on both sides and are therefore left out.
The price-to-rent ratio is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield and can only be classed as high or low in comparison with the current mortgage rate.

The incidental purchase costs, typically around 4.5% to just under 12% of the purchase price, are sunk costs from the moment the contract is notarised and make short holding periods expensive in arithmetical terms.
In the model case, buying only draws level with renting after ten years if the flat gains around 1.4% in value a year; that is achievable, but not a given.

begriffe.text: The purchase price divided by the annual net basic rent, and therefore the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A factor of 25 corresponds to 4%, a factor of 40 to 2.5%.

The annual net basic rent relative to the purchase price, calculated before incidental purchase costs and before all running costs. It serves as a quick indicator and is not a return in the investment sense.
The after-tax return that the equity tied up in the property would have earned elsewhere. If this item is missing from the comparison, the purchase appears cheaper than it is.

Amounts that are irretrievably lost once paid. With property, these are the incidental purchase costs. They do not increase the mortgage lending value and have to be earned back over the holding period.
The concentration of a large share of wealth in a single position. With an owner-occupied home, this position is also debt-financed, illiquid and tied to one location.
